t: Find the Minimum Number of Fibonacci Numbers Whose Sum Is K — Greedy Editorial
o: We must express k as a sum of Fibonacci numbers (repetition allowed) using as few terms as possible. For k = 7, the greedy pick 5 leaves 2, and 2 is itself Fibonacci, so the answer is 2. For k = 10, picking 8 leaves 2, again giving 2. For k = 19, picking 13 leaves 6; then 5 leaves 1, so we use 13 + 5 + 1 = 3 numbers. Since k can be up to 10^9 but there are only ~45 Fibonacci numbers up to that bound, any approach that repeatedly reduces k by the largest feasible Fibonacci number runs in a tiny number of steps.
k: Greedy works: always subtracting the largest Fibonacci number <= remaining k yields the minimum count.
There are only about 45 Fibonacci numbers up to 10^9, so precomputing or generating them on the fly is trivial.
The remainder after subtracting the largest Fibonacci f is always representable because consecutive Fibonacci gaps are small relative to f.

a.i: Treat it like coin change with Fibonacci numbers as coins: dp[x] = minimum numbers summing to x. This is intuitive but unnecessary since k can be 10^9, making O(k * 45) too slow in the worst case. It is included mainly to show why greedy is preferred. In practice for this problem's constraints the greedy below is strictly better.
s: Generate all Fibonacci numbers up to k.
Initialize dp[0] = 0 and dp[x] = infinity otherwise.
For each x from 1 to k, set dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - f]) over all Fibonacci f <= x.
a.t: O(k * 45) time — each of k states checks at most ~45 Fibonacci coins; too slow for k = 10^9 in strict settings.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy with Largest Fibonacci Subtraction
a.i: Always take the largest Fibonacci number f <= current k and replace k with k - f. This is optimal: if an optimal solution used two copies of some smaller Fibonacci g instead of one larger f where g1 + g2 <= f (two consecutive Fibonaccis sum to the next), those two could be merged into fewer terms. Repeatedly merging shows the greedy solution has minimal size. Since remainders shrink fast (roughly by a factor related to the golden ratio), only ~45 iterations are needed.
s: Set a = 1, b = 1 as the first two Fibonacci numbers.
While b <= k, advance the pair (a, b) = (b, a + b) so that a is the largest Fibonacci <= k when the loop ends.
Increment the answer counter and set k -= a.
a.t: O(log k) time — each outer iteration removes the largest Fibonacci, and the remainder shrinks geometrically (~45 iterations max for k <= 10^9).

w: In an interview, go straight to the greedy approach: generate Fibonacci numbers on the fly and repeatedly subtract the largest one not exceeding the remainder. The DP approach is worth mentioning briefly to justify why greedy is safe (two consecutive Fibonacci numbers sum to the next, so any solution using duplicates of smaller terms can be compressed). Pitfalls: forgetting to reset/advance the Fibonacci pair correctly inside the loop, integer overflow when computing the next Fibonacci near 10^9 (use 64-bit types in C++/Java), and off-by-one errors when finding the largest Fibonacci <= k. Edge cases: k = 1 returns 1, k = 2 returns 1 (single Fibonacci), k = 4 returns 2 (3 + 1). A common follow-up: prove the greedy is optimal, or handle queries for many k values (precompute the Fibonacci list once).
